Recap: Bag-of-Words and Word2vec

Recap: Bag-of-Words

Recap: one-hot encoding

Word embedding: turn words (and sentences) into numerical vectors.

Any problem with this model? There is no notion of similarity between words! (like and love are as different as any other pair.)

Distributional semantics

“You shall know a word by the company it keeps” (J. R. Firth 1957: 11)

The meaning of a word is given by the words that frequently appear close-by.

If two words predict similar neighbors, they mean similar things.

Speaker note: John Rupert Firth, English linguist. A very successful idea in NLP.

Word2vec: Skip-Gram Algorithm

Goal: maximize the probability of the real context words given the center word.

Binary classification task

\[\text{"Vaccines cause autism"} \;\rightarrow\; \mathbf{x} \;\rightarrow\; z = \alpha + \beta \mathbf{x} \;\rightarrow\; \phi(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\]

\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are model parameters.

Word embeddings we tried so far: - Bag-of-words (one-hot encoding) - Word2vec

Word2vec fails to capture context

Word2vec gives each word a single vector, regardless of the sentence it appears in.

“American shrew mole”, “One mole of carbon dioxide”, “Take a biopsy of the mole”: three different meanings, but one embedding.

Neural language model

How to build a neural language model?

  • Input: sequences of words, \(x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots, x_4\)
  • Output: probability distribution of the next word, \(P(x_i \mid x_1, \dots, x_{i-1})\)

Approach: let’s use a fixed window of context represented with word embeddings.

Neural language model – fixed window

Fixed-window based approach (similar idea to n-gram):

  • Words: \(x^{(1)}, x^{(2)}, x^{(3)}, x^{(4)}\)
  • Concatenated word embeddings: \(e = [e^{(1)}; e^{(2)}; e^{(3)}; e^{(4)}]\)
  • Hidden layer: \(h = f(We + b_1)\)
  • Output distribution: \(\hat{y} = \text{softmax}(Uh + b_2) \in \mathbb{R}^{|V|}\)

Neural language model – pros and cons

Improvements over n-gram LMs: - No sparsity problem - Don’t need to store all observed n-grams

Remaining problems: - Fixed window is too small - Increasing the window increases \(W\)

Language model evaluation

How do we define the quality of language models? Similar to word vector models, we define both extrinsic and intrinsic evaluation.

  • Extrinsic = validate on a specific task and measure accuracy (e.g., model A vs. B)
  • Intrinsic = measure model accuracy on an intermediate task
    • Measure accuracy of predicting words in an unseen test set
    • The metric for evaluation is perplexity
    • Gives a single metric for evaluating LMs

Intrinsic evaluation – motivation

Goal: model \(P(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n)\) or \(P(w_k \mid w_1, \dots, w_{k-1})\) accurately.

Shannon game: how well can we predict the next word? - I always order pizza with cheese and ______ - The 33rd president of the US was ______ - Once upon a ______

A better language model assigns higher probability to the word that actually occurs. How do we measure this?

WarningDCP1

Perplexity

A measure of how well a language model predicts the next word.

The intuition is that a good language model prefers “real” sentences over “rare” ones.

\[\text{Perplexity} = P(w_1, w_2, w_3, \dots, w_n)^{-1/n}\]

\[\text{Perplexity} = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i}^{n} \log P(w_i \mid w_1, \dots, w_{i-1})\right) \quad \text{(similar to cross-entropy)}\]

  • Lower score is better: minimizing perplexity ≈ maximizing the probability of the corpus
  • The score can be interpreted as an “average chance” of correctly assigning the next word

LM perplexity results

Training corpus 38 million words, test corpus 1.5 million words, both WSJ:

N-gram order Unigram Bigram Trigram
Perplexity (test) 962 170 109

Increasing n improves the model, but: - worsens the sparsity problem - and increases the model size

Improving neural language models

Many new architectures have been introduced to improve language models: - Recurrent neural networks (RNN) - Key idea is to use the same weights across layers - Long short-term memory (LSTM) - Transformers - Key idea is self-attention blocks - Generative pre-trained transformers (GPT)

Large language models

Large language model

  • A large language model (LLM) is a language model trained with self-supervised machine learning on a vast amount of text.
  • No need for labeled data!

The revolution: Transformers

Vaswani et al., “Attention Is All You Need” (2017).

Speaker note: 2017 paper, which has over 200k citations.

What does ChatGPT do?

  • GPT = Generative Pretrained Transformer
  • Next word prediction
  • This is not how we write!

By predicting the next word, the model must capture grammar, syntax, semantics, world knowledge, and some reasoning about context.

WarningDCP2

Transformer Architecture

The input (“Write a story.”) goes through tokenization, embedding and positional encoding, then through a series of transformer blocks, each made of an attention layer and a feedforward layer. A final softmax gives the output (“Once”).

Transformer Architecture: Attention

A word acquires more specific meaning from its surrounding words (context).

Context-aware embeddings (adjectives in this case):

This is a made-up example: we don’t know exactly what these attention mechanisms capture!

Attention step by step

1. Query: encoded in a matrix learned during training. Each noun “asks”: any adjectives in front of me?

2. Key matrix: “answers” the query.

3. To measure how well each key matches each query, take the dot product between the vectors (the slides say “cross product”; it is the dot product \(K_i \cdot Q_j\)).

4. Softmax transforms these into positive weights (each column sums to 1).

The model deduces which words are relevant to which other words. What now?

5. Update the embedding!

6. Value matrix: how to update the noun embedding.

We obtain a more “refined” word embedding:

In formula form (standard scaled dot-product attention):

\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\]

Transformer Architecture – overview

Application to the misinformation problem

Application to the misinformation problem

Use a pre-trained transformer as the encoder in the classification pipeline:

Two approaches:

Approach 1 (frozen encoder): - Create a sentence embedding by averaging pre-trained transformer word embeddings - Learn logistic regression parameters

Approach 2: fine-tune the transformer

Step Formula Note
Input \(x = (t_1, t_2, \dots, t_T)\)
Encoder \(h_T = f_\theta(x) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) transformer parameters \(\theta\)
Logits \(z = W h_T + b\) classification head
Predicted probs \(\hat{y} = \text{softmax}(z)\)
Loss \(\mathcal{L}(\theta, W, b) = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} y_k \log \hat{y}_k\)

The parameters of the transformer are only “slightly” tweaked to avoid catastrophic forgetting.

A bit of Giuseppe Ferro’s research

The persuasive power of vagueness

Joint work with Martino Lovisetto and Boris Koulevo (Alteca, France) and Somiya Schirokauer (Princeton University).

(Video embedded in the original slides.)

If I say “Chicago is a great place to be”…

You could infer: - Chicago is cheap - Chicago is fun - Chicago is safe - Etc.

By being vague, I have a higher chance of convincing you that Chicago is great, but I am not sure about what conclusions you are drawing.

Vagueness reduces epistemic vigilance through egocentric bias.

Too precise is easy to falsify. Too vague is not credible. Is there a sweet spot?

Research questions:

  • Is there an optimal level of vagueness for persuasion?
  • Does vagueness correlate with misinformation? If yes, can we use it to help identify misinformation?

Russell’s definition of vagueness

“A representation is vague when the relation of the representing system to the represented system is not one-one, but one-many… a photograph which is so smudged that it might equally represent Brown or Jones…”

“A vague belief has a much better chance of being true than a precise one, because there are more possible facts that would verify it. If I believe that so-and-so is tall, I am more likely to be right than if I believe that his height is between 6 ft. 2 in. and 6 ft. 3 in.”

Different flavors of vagueness

  • Degree vagueness
    • “Gloria is tall” is true iff \(\mu_{\text{height}}(\text{Gloria}) \geq t\) (for some unspecified threshold \(t\)).
    • “Gloria is taller than 185cm” is true iff \(\mu_{\text{height}}(\text{Gloria}) \geq 185\text{cm}\).
  • Approximation vagueness
    • “Around 20 people attended” is true iff \(x \in [20 - t, 20 + t]\).
  • Combinatorial vagueness
    • “Chicago is a great place to be” (many possible combinations of reasons could make it true).

Vagueness “predicts” misinformation?

Count vague words such as “around”, “about”, “almost”, “nearly”, “roughly”:

\[\text{Vagueness score} = \frac{\#\ \text{vague words}}{\#\ \text{words}}\]

But counting words misses context: “Between the 6-foot guy and the 5-foot guy, I prefer the tall one.” Here tall is not vague at all.

Guélorget, P., Icard, B., Gadek, G., Gahbiche, S., Gatepaille, S., Atemezing, G., & Égré, P. (2021, November). Combining vagueness detection with deep learning to identify fake news. In 2021 IEEE 24th International Conference on Information Fusion (FUSION) (pp. 1-8). IEEE.

Our vagueness quantifier

  1. Input sentence \(u\): “Chicago is a great place to be.”
  2. An LLM sharpening generator produces \(k\) precise readings: \(s_1\) “Chicago has a vibrant cultural scene”, \(s_2\) “The job opportunities in Chicago are plentiful”, \(s_3\) “Chicago is very affordable”.
  3. A semantic embedding module maps each reading to a vector \(\mathbf{e}_i\).
  4. Semantic distance computation: the more the readings disagree, the vaguer the sentence:

\[V(u) = \frac{2}{k(k-1)} \sum_{i<j} \bigl(1 - \cos(\mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j)\bigr)\]

Output vagueness for the example: \(V(u) = 0.8\).

Next steps

  • Check whether vagueness “predicts” misinformation.
  • Check the relationship between vagueness and persuasion (e.g. GoFundMe or lab experiments).
